They don't.

🔹 Agentic AI – AI that can plan, make decisions, use tools, and complete multi-step tasks with minimal human intervention.

✅ AI = The big umbrella

content:
My latest LinkedIn Learning course is out! This course focuses on leveraging MCP Server as a tool for building Power BI models.

We can use the generative AI capabilities of Power BI MCP Server as an assistant to build semantic models through natural language input prompts, starting with the Power Query interface. It can build ETL frameworks connecting to new data sources, edit existing queries, calculate new fields, and parameterize query inputs for scalability. It can also compare data tables between two queries in a single model or between two disparate models.

Once we load the data into the Power BI model, we can also use a connected MCP Server to add, edit, and parameterize DAX formulas. This includes bulk updates for editing DAX measure names, calculated formulas, and formatting. We can also use it to refactor DAX measure formulas and to create new calculation groups to improve model scalability.

As we build out our semantic models, we can utilize MCP Server to add descriptions to existing model entities like formulas. We can also generate markdown documents directly using the MCP Server within the IDE application for model documentation, skills, and agent instructions.

We can then utilize these skills and agent markdown files to build completely new semantic models constructed entirely via written input prompts connecting to generative AI models connected to Power BI MCP Server.

As I emphasized in the course (and in other content outside of it!), these models are probabilistic rather than deterministic, which means that even the most powerful models can still hallucinate and predict different results even with the same input prompts. There are some things, like bulk simultaneous formula and formatting updates that I found AI very efficient for, but there were also scenarios where it created far more problems and deleted entities both within models or project folders that I didn't otherwise want touched or certainly impacted.

As humans-in-the-loop, our knowledge therefore becomes even more crucial to know how to extract and scale the AI outcomes that do work for our model. It also becomes even more important to utilize versioning controls like Git to properly implement the desired target changes and to discard the otherwise futile ones.

Generative AI isn't the future anymore.

Last week, I watched two people solve the same problem.

The first spent nearly three hours writing a report from scratch.

The second finished in less than an hour.

The difference wasn't intelligence.

It wasn't experience.

It wasn't even technical skills.

The difference was how they used Generative AI.

One treated AI like Google.

The other treated it like a collaborator.

They asked AI to brainstorm ideas, organize their thoughts, review their writing, challenge assumptions, and refine the final output.

Notice what AI didn't do.

It didn't replace their thinking.

It accelerated it.

That's the part many people still misunderstand.

Generative AI isn't about pressing a button and letting a model do everything.

It's about reducing the time spent on repetitive work so you can focus on the decisions that actually require human judgment.

I've started using it in almost everything I build.
→ Turning rough notes into clear documentation.
→ Debugging code by exploring multiple approaches.
→ Summarizing long research papers before diving deeper.
→ Creating first drafts of presentations.
→ Generating SQL queries and then validating them.
→ Exploring different system design ideas before implementation.

Does AI get everything right?

Not even close.

It still hallucinates.

It misses context.

Sometimes it confidently gives the wrong answer.

That's why I never ask AI to think for me.

I ask it to think with me.

And that mindset has changed the way I work.

The people who will benefit the most from Generative AI won't be the ones chasing every new model.

They'll be the ones who know how to combine human experience, critical thinking, and AI into one effective workflow.

Technology changes.

Strong thinking doesn't.

Use AI to amplify your skills not replace them.

That's where the real advantage begins.

Deep Learning is a branch of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML). It uses Artificial Neural Networks, which work like the human brain, to learn from a large amount of data and make decisions without being explicitly programmed.

3. Improves itself by learning from mistakes.
4. Gives accurate predictions or decisions.

High accuracy
Learns automatically from data
Can process images, voice, and text
Improves performance with more data

Disadvantages:---

Needs a large amount of data
Requires powerful computers (GPU)

It doesn't learn exactly like humans. It learns mathematical patterns from data.

🤖 Deep Learning vs. Machine Learning: What's the Difference?

Machine Learning and Deep Learning are closely related, but they are not the same. Machine Learning is a subset of Artificial Intelligence (AI) that enables computers to learn patterns from data and make predictions without being explicitly programmed. It works best with structured data and often requires manual feature engineering. Deep Learning, on the other hand, is a specialized subset of Machine Learning that uses artificial neural networks with multiple hidden layers to automatically learn complex patterns from large amounts of data. It excels at tasks involving unstructured data such as images, videos, text, and audio, making it the technology behind applications like ChatGPT, facial recognition, speech assistants, and self-driving cars. While Machine Learning is faster to train and performs well with smaller datasets, Deep Learning typically requires more data, greater computing power, and longer training times—but often delivers higher accuracy for complex problems. Simply put, every Deep Learning model is a Machine Learning model, but not every Machine Learning model is Deep Learning.

💡 Key Takeaway: Choose Machine Learning for simpler prediction tasks with structured data, and Deep Learning for solving complex problems involving images, text, speech, and other unstructured data.

Most merchant processing failures don't happen because a card network goes down.

They happen because of single-point-of-failure routing architecture.
When transaction volume spikes, relying on static routing rules or a single primary processor is a guaranteed way to bleed revenue through false declines and processing limits.

True platform resilience in embedded finance isn't just about failover when a processor drops—it’s about dynamic, real-time multi-MID load balancing:
⚡ Pre-authorization risk checks: Scoring fraud signals before the transaction hits the rail. 
⚡ Smart routing logic: Directing transactions dynamically based on real-time approval rates, interchange costs, and MID caps. 
⚡ Automated decline recovery: Intelligent retry logic through secondary token vaults without adding customer latency.

If your payment infrastructure can't dynamically re-route traffic in real-time, you aren't just taking on operational risk—you're leaving 150–200 bps of processing yield on the table.

Build for resilience at the core ledger level, and processing uptime takes care of itself.

Which makes me think the real product in embedded finance shifts from the payment rail and the information display to the ability to delegate authority safely: scoped permissions, limits, an audit trail that lets you trust something else to pull the trigger.

content:
AI is compressing SaaS model from multiple directions at once. Software is dramatically cheaper to build, so a new entrant can show up with a sleeker AI-built tool, challenging incumbents. AI agents increasingly do the work that a person paying per-seat license used to do, putting pressure on traditional SaaS pricing model. 

Embedded finance presents a different way to monetize software. Instead of charging for seats, you take a share of the financial activity of your customers. Your platform's success and your customer's success are aligned. You are not dependent on AI model costs. And you are no longer competing for IT budget - you are tapping into operating budget of a business. 

Earlier this week, Jake Colognesi from Mamba Growth and I spent an hour with vertical software founders, CEOs, investors, embedded finance players and fintech operators, discussing the opportunity Embedded Finance represents for software companies in the age of AI. In this week's newsletter I summarized the key findings and insights from that session.

🏦 The History of Banking | Day 21: Online Banking – When the Bank Moved Into Your Home

There was a time when "going to the bank" meant exactly that.

Need to check your balance?

Drive to the branch.

Need to transfer money?

Stand in line.

Need a statement?

Wait for it to arrive in the mail.

Then the internet changed everything.

In the mid-1990s, banks began offering customers secure access to their accounts through a web browser. What started as a way to view balances quickly evolved into a complete digital banking experience.

For the first time, customers could manage their finances without stepping into a branch.

Online banking transformed the customer experience by making it possible to:

✔ View balances in real time
✔ Transfer funds instantly
✔ Pay bills electronically
✔ Download statements anytime
✔ Apply for loans and open accounts online

For banks, online banking was far more than a new channel.

It fundamentally changed expectations.

Customers no longer compared banks only to other banks—they compared them to every great digital experience they had online.

Convenience became a competitive advantage.

Speed became an expectation.

Digital experience became part of the brand.

Today, online banking has evolved into mobile apps, digital account opening, AI-powered support, and real-time payments.

Yet the goal remains unchanged:

Give customers secure, simple, and convenient access to their financial lives—wherever they are.

Perhaps the greatest lesson is this:

Branches made banking local.

The internet made banking available everywhere.

The future of banking isn't about choosing between digital and physical.

It's about creating experiences where customers can move seamlessly between both.

Today, the industry is experiencing one of the most significant transformations in its history. Digital banking is no longer just an alternative—it is becoming the foundation of financial services.

- Cloud-enabled infrastructure

For Pakistan, this transformation goes beyond convenience. It represents an opportunity to bring millions of unbanked individuals and SMEs into the formal financial system. With initiatives such as Raast, digital wallets, branchless banking, and emerging digital banks, the country is building the foundation for a more inclusive and efficient financial ecosystem.

However, digital transformation is not simply about replacing branches with mobile apps. It requires a cultural shift, stronger cybersecurity, advanced analytics, artificial intelligence, open banking frameworks, and continuous investment in customer trust and digital literacy.

The future belongs to banks that evolve from being transaction processors to becoming intelligent financial platforms—delivering personalized, secure, and seamless financial experiences across every digital touchpoint.

Pakistan's next competitive advantage will not be determined by the number of branches a bank owns, but by the quality of its digital ecosystem, innovation, and customer experience.

The journey from Brick-and-Mortar to Digital is no longer optional—it is the defining strategy for the future of banking in Pakistan.

content:
📌 Day 57/100
Why do some banks become a part of your life... while others remain just an account?

The answer isn't bigger branches or more products.

It's relationships.

Years ago, a bank's job was simple—open an account, approve a loan, and process transactions.

Today, that's no longer enough.

The best banks are quietly changing their role.

Instead of asking, "What product can we sell?"

They're asking, "How can we become part of this customer's financial journey?"

It often starts with one product—a salary account or a home loan.

From there, the relationship grows.

Savings accounts, insurance, credit cards, investments, business banking, and wealth management all become part of one connected ecosystem.

At the same time, another transformation is happening behind the scenes.

Customers don't see it, but AI and Zero-Ops are helping banks verify documents, process transactions, and complete routine tasks in minutes instead of hours.

That means better customer experience, lower operating costs, and the ability to grow without adding the same level of expenses.

To me, this is one of the most underappreciated changes in Indian banking.

The future may not belong to the bank with the most branches.

It may belong to the bank that builds the strongest relationships—and uses technology to 
serve millions of customers efficiently.

content:
Many entrepreneurs focus only on their credit score, but overlook something just as important—their banking history.

If you've been reported to ChexSystems, you may have difficulty opening a traditional checking account at some banks. Without an active banking relationship, you're also limiting your future opportunities for business loans, lines of credit, and other banking products from those institutions.

That's why it's important to rebuild your banking profile. Even if you can't qualify for a checking account right away, some banks and credit unions may allow you to open a savings account or offer second-chance banking programs. Establishing that relationship can be the first step toward rebuilding trust with the institution.

Funding isn't just about your credit score—it's about your entire financial profile. Banks look at how you manage your accounts, your cash flow, your deposit history, and the relationship you've built over time.

Don't wait until you need capital to start building relationships. The strongest funding approvals often begin with a simple bank account opened months—or even years—before the application.

47 million payments moved through Yapily in the last 12 months. Almost nobody who made one has heard of us.

That is by design.

Open banking is like Italy, where quality is found in the detail. The grind of the coffee. The stitching inside a jacket that no one ever sees. Only the people who make them notice a perfect seam. The jacket simply hangs well, and you never think about why.

The work that matters is unglamorous: consent flows that hold up under audit, the quiet resilience of connections that hold steady while the banks behind them change, the reconciliation that just works at 2am while everyone sleeps.

Years of that work now look like 2,000 bank connections across 19 markets, 721 million API calls in a year, and a business that reached profitability without a victory lap.

The next era of finance will be built by agents acting on our behalf, and it will run on whichever infrastructure got the details right. When the thing being moved is someone's money, there is no partial credit.

Boring, in infrastructure, is a compliment.

And it's one that's getting much more important as AI is unleashed on financial data.

UPI transformed how India moves money. But it also transformed our expectations.

Instant payments are no longer a differentiator.  They are the baseline.

The next phase of digital payments feels less about moving money faster and more about making payments invisible within everyday experiences.

Embedded finance, Cross-border payments, Programmable payments, AI-driven financial experiences. These could define what comes next.

It's interesting to see the conversation shifting from building the best payment rails to building the smartest financial experiences on top of them.

The infrastructure has matured. The real innovation may now lie in how we use it.

It makes me wonder if the future of digital payments will be measured less by transaction volumes and more by the value created around every transaction.
